claims.text: The proposed starting material is a mixed elemental powder blend containing refractory elements and Cu.
LPBF of the mixed powder will enable large-scale in situ reaction synthesis.
LPBF will form a stable, homogeneous refractory-element/Cu composite microstructure.
Rapid heating and cooling during LPBF minimizes segregation associated with positive refractory-element/Cu heats of mixing.
A positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu creates a thermodynamic drive for phase segregation.
High-energy laser scanning in an inert atmosphere produces rapid melting and solidification.
LPBF produces a fine nanocrystalline or lamellar microstructure at refractory-phase/Cu interfaces.
The localized energy input of LPBF promotes rapid diffusion and reaction between refractory elements and Cu.
LPBF-induced diffusion and reaction counteract segregation and stabilize the composite microstructure.
The resulting composite will have uniformly distributed constituent phases.
The LPBF composite will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally processed alloys.
The LPBF composite will have greater irradiation resistance than conventionally processed alloys.
The LPBF composite will have greater thermal stability than conventionally processed alloys.
The predicted property combination would make the composite suitable for next-generation nuclear reactor applications.
Conventional melting or arc melting of refractory elements with Cu typically produces substantial segregation and unstable microstructures.
The claimed benefits require optimization of laser power, scanning speed, reaction completion, and solidification rate.
Departures from the optimized LPBF processing window may cause incomplete mixing or defect formation.
The precise LPBF processing window and industrial scalability remain unresolved.
A controlled comparison of LPBF and conventional melting can test differences in segregation, microstructural homogeneity, mechanical properties, and thermal stability.
